Family Health

Breast pain: common causes and when to seek care

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Breast pain can be unsettling, especially when you wonder whether it means cancer. The medical term is mastalgia, and it includes anything from mild sensitivity to a heavy, burning or sharp ache. Pain alone is usually not a sign of breast cancer. Still, its timing, location and accompanying changes matter: a new lump, persistent focal pain or an inflamed breast deserves assessment rather than reassurance based on pain alone.

Notice the pattern before naming the cause

Breast tissue changes as hormones change. Development during puberty, monthly menstrual cycles, pregnancy and the transition to menopause can all affect tenderness. Some discomfort follows a repeating monthly pattern, called cyclic pain. Noncyclic pain has no consistent relationship with periods and may arise in the breast itself or in nearby muscles, ribs or other tissues.

Describe what you actually feel: soreness when touched, fullness, tingling, a pulling sensation or a more concentrated burning or stabbing pain. Note whether it affects one or both breasts, one small area or a wider region. The intensity does not identify the cause by itself; severe discomfort can have a benign explanation, while an important breast change may cause little pain.

How menstrual hormones can affect the breasts

Changes in estrogen and progesterone across the cycle can leave breasts feeling fuller, lumpier or tender before a period. This commonly affects both sides and can extend toward the armpits. Symptoms often ease when bleeding begins or shortly afterward. Some people notice only a few uncomfortable days, while others have symptoms for longer; there is no universal two- or three-day timetable.

A diary over one or two cycles can help reveal the pattern. Record period dates, the location and severity of pain, its effect on sleep or activity and any medicine changes. Hormonal pain often settles after menopause, although hormone treatment can influence symptoms. Worsening pain is not an inevitable consequence of age. Do not wait for a completed diary before seeking help with a new lump or other concerning change.

Cysts and fibrocystic changes are not all the same

A cyst is a fluid-filled pocket in the breast. Some are too small to feel; others form a noticeable lump and can become uncomfortable as they enlarge. Fibrosis refers to fibrous tissue changes. The term fibrocystic changes is often used for a combination of lumpiness, cysts and tenderness that may fluctuate with the menstrual cycle. Lumpy or tender areas may be more noticeable in the upper outer breast, but location alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

A simple cyst and ordinary fibrosis do not themselves increase breast-cancer risk. That reassurance applies to an assessed finding, not to every unexplained lump. Imaging can distinguish a simple fluid-filled cyst from a solid mass or a more complex cystic abnormality, which may need further investigation. Cysts are not simply proof that aging breast tissue has turned into fat, and a new lump should not be diagnosed by touch at home.

Breast lumpiness is different from mammographic density

Dense breasts contain proportionally more glandular and fibrous tissue and less fat on a mammogram. A person cannot reliably determine this by how firm or lumpy a breast feels. Fibrocystic symptoms and a report of dense breasts therefore should not be used as interchangeable descriptions.

Density matters for two separate reasons: dense tissue can hide an abnormality on mammography, and it is also associated with higher breast-cancer risk. If an imaging report mentions density, discuss its meaning alongside your other risk factors and local screening guidance. This does not mean a tender or lumpy breast is cancerous, nor does it mean routine mammography is useless.

During breastfeeding, start with attachment and engorgement

Pain during a feed may be related to how the baby is positioned and attached. Repeated rubbing or compression of the nipple can leave it sore or cracked. Ask a midwife, lactation professional or other trained clinician to watch a feed rather than assuming persistent pain is something you must tolerate. A blister, rash or ongoing burning sensation may need its own assessment; appearance alone does not prove infection.

Engorgement means the breasts are overly full and feel firm, tight and uncomfortable. It may occur as milk first comes in or after a longer interval without feeding. Fullness can also make attachment harder. Offer feeds in response to the baby’s cues and seek support if milk transfer is difficult. If needed, expressing a small amount for comfort can help; repeatedly pumping to make the breasts completely empty can encourage excess production.

Recognize inflammation and possible mastitis

Mastitis involves inflammation and does not always begin as a bacterial infection. It may cause a hot, swollen, painful area, sometimes with fever, chills or a flu-like feeling. Skin redness can be less obvious on darker skin. Antibiotics are appropriate in some cases, but are not automatically the treatment for every sore nipple or episode of fullness.

Continue comfortable, responsive feeding when possible and obtain advice on expression if feeding is difficult. Rest, a cool compress and nonrestrictive support may help. Avoid forceful massage, rolling hard pressure toward the nipple or extra pumping beyond the baby’s needs. Contact a clinician if symptoms fail to improve within 12–24 hours of home care, sooner if you feel very unwell. Mastitis-like symptoms when you are not breastfeeding also need assessment.

Muscles, breast size, injuries and surgery can contribute

The discomfort may come from outside the breast. Gardening, rowing, heavy lifting or another unfamiliar activity can strain chest muscles. Pain from the chest wall, shoulder, neck or back may be felt in the breast area. Tell the clinician whether movement or pressing on a particular spot reproduces it, but do not use this observation alone to rule out another cause.

Larger breasts can add strain and be accompanied by neck, shoulder or back discomfort. A well-fitting bra or activity-appropriate support may improve comfort. An injury can also leave localized tenderness. After breast surgery, pain related to scars or healing tissues can persist after the surface wound has closed. New, increasing or unexplained postoperative pain should be discussed with the treating team.

Review medicines and everyday factors without blaming yourself

Some hormonal contraceptives, menopausal hormone treatments, certain antidepressants, some blood-pressure medicines and some antibiotics can be associated with breast pain. This does not mean all medicines in those groups cause it. Bring the exact names, doses and timing to an appointment. A clinician may consider whether a change would help; do not abruptly stop a prescribed treatment.

Smoking is associated with some breast problems, including non-breastfeeding inflammation, and support to stop is worthwhile. A specific adrenaline explanation should not be presented as an established cause of your pain. Similarly, research on changing dietary fat, caffeine or other foods is limited or inconsistent. A balanced eating pattern is reasonable, but breast pain is not evidence that you ate the wrong food, and diet changes should not replace evaluation of a new symptom.

When breast pain needs a clinical appointment

Arrange an assessment if pain is worsening, repeatedly affects the same small area, interferes with usual activities or continues for more than a couple of weeks without a clear improving pattern. Do not treat two weeks as a required waiting period. A new breast or armpit lump, thickened area, change in breast shape, skin dimpling, a new inverted nipple, persistent nipple rash or unexplained discharge warrants review even when painless.

A hot, swollen breast with fever or chills needs prompt advice. Pregnancy and breastfeeding do not make a persistent lump or skin change safe to ignore. Most breast pain has a noncancerous cause, but pain can occur with cancer too. Clinical assessment, rather than whether a lump hurts, is what separates reassuring changes from those needing investigation.

Separate a breast symptom from an emergency chest symptom

Chest pressure, squeezing or tightness may be felt near the breast but can have a different cause. Call your local emergency number for suspected heart-attack symptoms, especially pain spreading to an arm, neck or jaw, severe breathlessness, collapse or abnormal responsiveness. Sweating, nausea or an indigestion-like sensation may accompany it. You do not need to have every symptom, and arm tingling is not a requirement.

Do not drive yourself to emergency care if a heart attack is suspected. Follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions. A breast-pain diary, a trial of a different bra or a routine clinic appointment should not delay urgent assessment of acute chest symptoms.

What to expect at an assessment

A clinician will ask when the pain began, whether it is constant or intermittent, how it relates to periods and what makes it better or worse. Be ready to describe its quality and severity, point to the painful area and explain its effect on sleep or daily life. Mention pregnancy or breastfeeding, previous breast problems or surgery, family history and all medicines and supplements.

An examination helps determine whether the finding seems to arise from breast tissue or nearby structures. A reassuring initial assessment should come with a plan: how to manage symptoms, when to return and what changes should trigger earlier review. Continue any screening appropriate for your age and risk, but report a new symptom rather than waiting for a routine screening invitation.

Why imaging, aspiration and biopsy answer different questions

Not everyone with breast pain needs a scan. Diffuse pain that follows the cycle, with no suspicious findings, often does not require additional diagnostic imaging just for the pain. Persistent focal symptoms may prompt ultrasound or diagnostic mammography, chosen according to age, examination and circumstances. Ultrasound is commonly the first investigation in younger people; pregnancy and lactation should be mentioned when tests are arranged.

Ultrasound can help show whether an area contains fluid or is solid. A clinician may drain a painful simple cyst with a needle to relieve pressure; it can sometimes refill. Tissue biopsy samples an abnormality when its nature needs clarification and is different from simply withdrawing cyst fluid. MRI has selected uses but is not a routine next step for every episode of tenderness or every cyst.

Start relief with comfort and appropriate pain medicine

Choose a supportive bra that fits without digging in. Some people prefer a soft bra at night; others are more comfortable without one. Wearing a tight bra around the clock is not a universal treatment. Adjust activities that clearly aggravate symptoms while an injury settles, and use a cool compress if it feels soothing.

Ask a pharmacist or clinician about a suitable pain reliever. Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, is not an anti-inflammatory drug; ibuprofen belongs to the NSAID group. The choice depends on pregnancy, other illnesses, medicines and the intended route of use. Do not assume an oral medicine and a medicated gel are interchangeable or suitable for application where a baby feeds. Follow the product instructions and individualized advice rather than combining products that may contain the same ingredient.

Supplements and hormone treatments need realistic expectations

Routine calcium supplements, cutting salt sharply or taking vitamins should not be presented as proven cures for breast pain. Evidence for vitamin E or evening primrose oil is limited, and supplements can interact with medicines. If you want to try a dietary change, keep it manageable, observe whether it actually helps and maintain adequate nutrition.

Changing a hormonal contraceptive or menopausal treatment sometimes helps, although the same types of medicines can also provoke symptoms. Severe persistent pain may occasionally warrant specialist treatment such as tamoxifen after simpler measures have failed. Such treatment has important risks and is not a self-care option or a medicine to borrow. Noncyclic pain needs treatment matched to its cause, rather than an automatic hormonal remedy.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The clinical pattern helps distinguish menstrual tenderness, cysts, lactation problems and pain from nearby structures.

Independent breast-health and radiology guidance supports targeted assessment rather than routine imaging for all pain.

Dietary and supplement evidence is limited; treatment safety depends on individual circumstances.

How BeMama can help

This full English adaptation preserves the written article’s causes, diagnostic discussion and treatment topics while correcting outdated lactation advice and clarifying cancer-risk terminology.

When to seek help

For education, not diagnosis. Seek prompt assessment of new breast changes and urgent help for severe illness or acute chest symptoms. Clinical breast-health and lactation review remains pending before publication.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Track the pattern of pain, but seek assessment promptly for a new lump, skin or nipple change.
  • Simple cysts and fibrocystic lumpiness differ from mammographic density and from suspicious breast abnormalities.
  • Breastfeeding pain deserves practical support; forceful massage and excessive pumping can worsen problems.
  • Tests and treatment should follow the clinical findings, not a fixed checklist for every painful breast.
  • Acute pressure-like chest pain or severe breathing difficulty needs emergency attention.

Frequently asked questions

Does breast pain mean I have breast cancer?

Usually it has another cause, particularly when it follows a menstrual pattern. However, cancer can sometimes be painful. A new lump, persistent focal pain or a skin or nipple change should be checked regardless of whether it hurts.

How long should I keep a breast-pain diary?

One or two cycles may help show a repeating pattern. Record timing, location, severity and medicines. Do not postpone an appointment for a concerning new change just to finish the diary.

Are lumpy breasts the same as dense breasts?

No. Lumpiness is something you may feel; density is a description based on mammographic appearance. An imaging report and your overall risk profile help determine what breast density means for you.

Can a painful cyst be drained?

Sometimes. A clinician may use needle aspiration to relieve a confirmed fluid-filled cyst. A solid or complex abnormality may instead need other tests or tissue sampling, so first establish what the lump is.

Should I pump until an engorged breast feels empty?

Repeated extra pumping can stimulate more milk. Feed responsively and ask for help with attachment and milk transfer. Small amounts of expression for comfort, or an individualized expression plan when the baby cannot feed effectively, are more appropriate.

Does every case of mastitis need antibiotics?

No. Inflammation is not always bacterial infection. Seek advice if you are very unwell or fail to improve after 12–24 hours of home measures; a clinician can decide whether antibiotics or another assessment is needed.

Could a medicine be responsible for my breast pain?

Possibly. Hormones and some other prescriptions can contribute. Review the exact medicine and the timing of symptoms with a clinician or pharmacist rather than stopping treatment on your own.

Do I need ultrasound, a mammogram and MRI?

Not routinely. The examination, symptom pattern, age and other circumstances guide testing. Some people need no additional imaging for cyclic pain; others need targeted diagnostic investigation.

Will calcium or evening primrose oil cure the pain?

Neither should be promised as a reliable cure. Check supplement safety and interactions, and focus on an assessment of persistent symptoms and measures suited to the cause.

Can I wait two weeks before reporting a new breast lump?

A two-week symptom threshold is not a rule for lumps. Arrange an assessment when you notice a new lump or other concerning breast change. Acute chest pressure or severe breathlessness belongs in an emergency pathway.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
